title: Conditional participation in mainstream SEND : Documentary analysis of participation sustainability in statutory assessment narratives
abstract: Abstract Inclusive education policy often infers educational access from observable indicators such as attendance, engagement and behavioural compliance, yet visible participation may not indicate whether engagement is sustainable across contexts or over time. Participation sustainability is defined here as the extent to which engagement can be maintained across settings and over time without disproportionate cognitive, emotional or sensory cost. This study examined whether indicators of participation sustainability could be systematically identified within statutory multi‐professional assessment narratives used to inform provision decisions. A mixed‐methods documentary analysis was conducted on 21 anonymised cases drawn from statutory assessment materials for pupils aged 7–14 in mainstream settings, spanning a range of categories of need. Evidence from Education, Health and Care Plans, professional reports and school documentation was coded using a framework capturing environmental dependence, regulatory cost, contextual variability, transition vulnerability and temporal fragility. title: Syndroming: When difference becomes diagnosis
abstract: Abstract In this article, I examine ‘syndroming’: the expansion and institutionalisation of diagnostic framings of school difficulty in contemporary education systems. Drawing on accounts of classification and critiques of medicalisation and mental health discourse, I argue that current policy arrangements in England—particularly those associated with Education Health and Care Plans and tribunal processes—create incentives to describe children's difficulties in clinical terms. In such contexts, complex and context‐dependent experiences are translated into recognised categories that function as gateways to support. I contextualise the local case in the international circulation of diagnostic frameworks and their role in shaping local practices. I conclude that while diagnostic categories have an important place, their expanding use risks narrowing how difficulty is understood, with implications for inclusive education.

title: Teachers' challenges and instructional experiences in supporting young learners with dyslexia: Implications for inclusive teaching in mainstream primary schools in Zimbabwe
abstract: Abstract Teachers play a pivotal role in supporting learners with dyslexia. However, a considerable number of mainstream schools continue to encounter significant challenges in creating truly inclusive learning environments. The study aims to explore the challenges and instructional experiences of primary school teachers in supporting learners with dyslexia in mainstream classrooms, and how these shape their capacity to implement inclusive education practices. An Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis research design was chosen, using a convenience sampling technique to select 20 mainstream teachers of learners with dyslexia from Chivi district in Zimbabwe. Individual semi‐structured interviews were used to obtain data. The interviews examined teachers' experiences, training backgrounds, support systems and perceptions of inclusive education. Data were analysed inductively to identify recurring challenges and opportunities for strengthening inclusive teaching practices. Teachers identified several barriers to effectively supporting learners with dyslexia, including limited specialised training, low awareness of the condition and insufficient institutional support. Teachers' awareness of pedagogical learning needs of children with autism spectrum disorder in special primary schools in Tanzania
abstract: Abstract This study explores teachers' awareness of the pedagogical learning needs of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in special primary schools in Tanzania. Twelve teachers from six special primary schools who teach children with ASD were purposively sampled. The study used semi‐structured interviews to collect data and applied thematic analysis. The findings revealed that teachers perceived that children with ASD require multimodal communication, social skills development, sensory processing support and assistive technology to learn effectively. The study also found that teachers experience challenges in identifying the pedagogical learning needs of these children due to limited knowledge of appropriate pedagogical practices. Therefore, the study recommends that teachers engage in ongoing professional development focused on ASD through seminars, workshops and short training sessions to enhance their capacity to address each child's pedagogical learning needs effectively.

title: Inclusion bases and the improvement of special educational needs and disability provision in schools: Panacea or policy‐patching?
When participation breaks down: Parent and child accounts of the development of emotionally based school avoidance in autistic pupils
abstract: Abstract Emotionally based school avoidance (EBSA) refers to persistent difficulties attending school associated with significant emotional distress. Autistic pupils appear to experience EBSA at elevated rates, yet little research has examined how these difficulties develop over time. This study explored the developmental trajectory of EBSA through qualitative analysis of specialist educational consultation transcripts relating to 30 autistic pupils aged 10–14 attending mainstream schools in the United Kingdom, all of whom had sustained attendance difficulties. Thematic analysis identified a recurring developmental pattern. Early stages were characterised by masked distress and sustained efforts to cope with demanding school environments. Over time, cumulative pressures including sensory overload, social challenges and anxiety contributed to escalating distress. Attendance difficulties were often initially interpreted behaviourally, delaying supportive responses. Findings highlight the importance of recognising masked distress and addressing environmental stressors early to prevent escalating school participation difficulties.

title: Social networks in special schools: Friendships, bullying and play among pupils with special educational needs and disabilities
abstract: Abstract Little is known about the social networks of children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) in specialist school settings—schools designed to support specific educational needs. Most literature on the social connections of children with SEND suggests that they have fewer friendships and are more involved in bullying situations, but these data are usually collected from mainstream school settings, where children with SEND are the minority. To better understand the social connections of pupils with SEND in specialist school settings, we conducted a social network study in this educational context. Specifically, this research studied whole‐school social networks in three special schools with differing specialisms: (1) social, emotional and mental health; (2) cognition and learning; and (3) autism. Positive peer networks (friends and play companions) and negative peer networks (bullying and victimisation) largely mirrored the social networks of mainstream schools, although there was less student hierarchy. title: Alone in the group room
abstract: Abstract In Sweden, an underexplored educational practice involves pupils being placed outside the classroom to receive individual instruction while remaining formally enrolled in a regular class. Although widely used, this form of provision has received limited research attention. Drawing on a care‐ethical perspective, this study examines how 16 upper primary schoolteachers and special educators describe and reason about such arrangements. The analysis focuses on how the purpose of the instruction is understood and how its implications for pupils' relationships with classmates and teachers are articulated. The findings indicate a contrast between short‐term, knowledge‐oriented forms of instruction and more prolonged forms of separation motivated by social concerns. While the former were generally described as purposeful and limited in scope, the latter were associated with ambivalence and ethical unease. Across participants' accounts, decisions to remove pupils from the classroom were often shaped by efforts to avoid situations perceived as socially difficult. title: ‘The biggest conversation in a generation’? A critical discourse analysis of the UK government's national conversation on England's SEND reform
abstract: Abstract This study was conducted as a rapid response to the UK government's announcement of a ‘national conversation’ on England's special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) reforms, prior to the publication of the English Schools White Paper in early 2026. The announcement of the ‘national conversation’ initiative was met with scepticism from advocacy groups and sector commentators, who questioned both the purpose of the exercise and the conditions under which participation would take place. Using a Critical Policy Discourse Analysis framework, this study analysed a data corpus of the national conversation texts to explore the discursive articulation of the government’s intended policy directions, and how the initiative was enacted as a policy process in advance of formal reform consultation. Our analysis resulted in the following findings: (1) The initiative worked to construct legitimacy of policy direction, (2) The National Conversation was discursively constructed as metaphorical rather than reciprocal and (3) Children and young people received only symbolic inclusion in the initiative despite being positioned as central figures in the public engagement process. title: Broadening participation: Measuring the mental health of pupils with special educational needs and disabilities
abstract: Abstract Pupils in non‐mainstream settings, including special schools and alternative provision, are rarely included in large‐scale school‐based mental health surveys. As a result, the needs and experiences of children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) are often absent from population‐level data. This study assessed the feasibility of delivering an adapted school‐based mental health survey in non‐mainstream settings, provided an initial snapshot of pupils' mental health and wellbeing and explored whether adult support during survey completion influenced responses. A shortened, accessibility adapted version of the OxWell Student Survey, including audiovisual read‐aloud support and flexible administration, was completed by 296 pupils aged 8–18 across 15 non‐mainstream schools in England. Descriptive analyses summarised school experience, bullying, loneliness, mental health, self‐harm and support pathways. Exploratory comparisons examined differences between pupils who completed the survey independently and those who received adult support. title: Saudi education teachers' evaluation of their Government's initiative to promote inclusive education
abstract: Abstract This descriptive study, rooted in a constructivist perspective, delves into the perceptions of the benefits and challenges of implementing inclusion education practices in Saudi Arabia as articulated by 56 preservice female general education teachers. Participants were queried on their preferences for inclusive or restricted classroom placements for students with special needs, along with the reasons underlying their choices. Five themes have been derived from the coding process: greater educational opportunities; acceptance by outside communities; positive social and emotional outcomes; opportunities to learn from each other; and greater self‐acceptance. Results showcased a majority preference for inclusive classroom settings, with varied rationales aligning with the identified themes. Those favouring restricted settings emphasised tailored academic environments and protection from potential failures. A subset endorsed both settings, promoting social and emotional development in inclusive settings and academic development in restrictive settings. title: Neurodiversity and strengths‐based approaches in education: A Walker and Avant concept analysis
abstract: Abstract Neurodiversity and strengths‐based approaches are increasingly prominent in educational discourse, reflecting the ongoing evolution of inclusive educational practice. Each concept is subject to its own definitional ambiguity and has attracted a range of critiques. These unresolved issues at the ideational level risk undermining their effective application in practice. For example, theoretical questions concerning whether the two are distinct or overlapping have prompted models for their conceptual integration. Clarifying these relationships is therefore essential to support meaningful and consistent implementation in education. This study reports a Walker and Avant concept analysis for each term, aiming to map and clarify how the concepts are used within educational research. The focus was on exploring modern, contextualised understandings rather than relying solely on reified, original academic definitions. A subsequent comparative analysis of the two concept analyses was then conducted to determine whether systematic research evidence supports previous proposals for integration. title: Parent and carer perspectives on specialist speech and language therapy assessments for children and young people with down syndrome
abstract: Abstract Children and young people with Down syndrome (DS) exhibit distinct speech and language profiles and are frequently referred to speech and language therapy (SALT) services. These may lack specialised DS knowledge, potentially bridged with a SALT assessment by DS specialists. However, these assessments are not universally available, and this study aimed to explore the perspectives of parents and carers who underwent such an assessment; specifically, their motivation, perception of the outcomes and the broader impact. A mixed‐methods study was conducted with 35 parents and carers completing an online questionnaire. Challenges with SALT provision and DS‐specific knowledge of local services were reported as motivating factors in seeking a specialist assessment, often conveying the personal toll and cost of obtaining these. Participants reported that the assessment facilitated their understanding of the child's SALT needs, reflecting empowerment. Positive outcomes post‐assessment were reported, reflected in the significant difference between satisfaction levels with the Education, Health and Care Plan. title: Parental perceptions of the education of their children with Down syndrome: Starting points for cultural change
abstract: Abstract The framework proposed in this paper was developed as part of a research project which sought the perspectives of parents on the educational experiences of their children with Down syndrome. The narrative research involved unstructured interviews with ten parents of children and young people with Down syndrome, in England. Interview transcripts were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings were interpreted in the light of previous research and theoretical perspectives which affirm human variation and unbounded views of competence. The resulting framework illustrates the interconnectedness of systemic and cultural change and suggests that a multifaceted approach is necessary to achieve a consistently positive and inclusive educational experience for children with Down syndrome. Key areas are identified in which practitioners can make changes which will contribute to developing inclusive practice. It is argued that fundamental to sustainable change are presumptions of belonging and competence in addition to a professional willingness to learn. title: Developing entrepreneurial capabilities for people with disabilities
abstract: Abstract People with disabilities face many barriers in education, business and employment. Although previous studies have identified several personal and entrepreneurial traits as important competencies, limited research has examined how these traits support individuals with different disabilities in becoming entrepreneurs. This study investigates whether people with visual, hearing and physical disabilities perceive these traits similarly and whether their attitudes towards risk‐taking, ambiguity, achievement motivation and proactive decision‐making vary by disability type. This quantitative study used a survey questionnaire administered to prospective entrepreneurs with disabilities in colleges, universities and business settings in Oman. Of the 100 responses collected, 90 were included in the analysis, with equal representation of participants with visual, hearing and physical impairments. The seven traits—risk‐taking, innovativeness, self‐control, motivation, self‐efficacy, tolerance of ambiguity and proactive decision‐making—were found to be important, but they do not alone explain entrepreneurial intention. title: Educators' knowledge and misconceptions about dyslexia: Implications for teacher training and practice
abstract: Abstract Dyslexia is a common specific learning difficulty that can affect academic performance and students' educational experiences. Despite its prevalence in primary education, delays in identification are still reported, sometimes associated with educators' misconceptions and limited knowledge about the condition. Understanding educators' beliefs and knowledge may help inform the design of professional training programs, particularly in non‐English‐speaking contexts such as Spain, where research on this topic remains limited. The present study examined Spanish educators' knowledge of dyslexia, focusing on scientific understanding, misconceptions, and potential differences among professional groups, including speech‐language pathologists (SLPs), therapeutic specialists and primary school teachers. It also explored the relationships between training, confidence, professional experience and exposure to students with dyslexia and overall knowledge scores. title: Establishing expert consensus on the development and implementation of a Whole School Approach to supporting primary school children with dyslexia: A Delphi study
abstract: Abstract Dyslexia affects an estimated 7%–10% of children and can have a profound and lasting impact on literacy, academic attainment and wellbeing. In Northern Ireland, provision for children with dyslexia remains inconsistent, characterised by variation in identification procedures, delays in assessment and uneven support across schools. A Whole School Approach (WSA) offers a strategic and sustainable model for embedding dyslexia‐inclusive practice across all aspects of school life. This study aimed to achieve expert consensus on the essential components of a WSA to support primary school children with dyslexia. A modified two‐round Delphi design was employed with 40 international experts, including educational psychologists, SENCos, specialist teachers, researchers and policymakers. Round 1 comprised 60 items across seven domains (development, components, leadership, parental involvement, training, progress assessment and barriers). Round 2 refined 11 items based on feedback. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and interquartile ranges, while qualitative feedback was analysed thematically. Consensus was defined as ≥70% agreement. title: ‘I really like being on the floor, because I spend all the time in my chair’: Children with disabilities' experiences of physical activity in school
abstract: Abstract Children with multiple disabilities often encounter significant barriers to participating in physical activity, impacting not only their physical health but also their overall experience in school. This study places the voices of four children at the centre of their own research, exploring their lived experiences of participating in physical activity in school. Using the Mosaic approach, this child‐centred participatory study shows how children take part and engage with physical activity as part of their school day. Using videos and photography, child‐led tours and ethically sensitive conversations with researchers, children shared a range of opportunities for enjoyment, exploration and interactions with others as well as challenges such as restricted access and limited equipment. Their narratives highlight the urgent need for inclusive practices to be informed by children and young people with physical and cognitive impairments. This study contributes to the growing body of research advocating for children's voice in education and health and offers key insights for education and health practitioners aiming to promote inclusive, health‐supportive physical activity opportun

title: Bridging spaces towards inclusion: Inclusive pedagogy in disability‐specific after‐school centres ( KDAP ‐ AMEA ) in Greece
abstract: Abstract Centres for Creative Occupation for People with Disabilities (KDAP‐AMEA) are disability‐specific after‐school structures in Greece operating within the broader framework of inclusive education and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Grounded in rights‐based principles that emphasise participation, agency, and equal access, this qualitative study explores how special educators working in KDAP‐AMEA conceptualise and enact inclusive pedagogy, the challenges they encounter, and the structural conditions shaping their practice. Semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 12 educators across multiple regions and analysed thematically. Findings indicate that educators frame inclusion primarily as meaningful participation, relational belonging, and the cultivation of agency through collaborative and experiential practices. Participants reported enhanced peer interaction, communication, confidence, and socio‐emotional development among children. title: Autism‐friendly modern foreign language teaching in a university setting: Towards a toolkit for teaching second languages to autistic students
abstract: Abstract This paper summarises the findings of a research project at a British university exploring autistic students studying modern foreign languages (MFL). The project investigates the experiences, motivations, learning strategies and preferences of autistic MFL learners in a Higher Education context to better understand how MFL classroom pedagogy can be designed more inclusively. This interdisciplinary study combines pedagogic, clinical linguistic and anthropological perspectives. This study, which is based on the analysis of semi‐structured interviews and focus groups, suggests that specific types of language classroom settings, activities and linguistic content disadvantage autistic learners. While autistic students appreciated approaches that supported their individual learning preferences, certain routine aspects of established MFL pedagogy—such as spontaneous improvisation in a target language—increased anxiety and led to declared non‐attendance. Drawing on these findings, we provide recommendations to prevent or mitigate their impact. Inclusion perspectives among Arab special education teachers in Israel
abstract: Abstract This qualitative study explores the lived experiences of Arab special education (SPED) teachers in Israel who support the inclusion of students with learning disabilities in mainstream classrooms. Drawing on in‐depth semi‐structured interviews with ten SPED teachers, the study examines challenges related to professional preparation, instructional practice and systemic support within culturally and structurally complex educational contexts. The findings indicate a persistent gap between theoretical knowledge acquired in academic training and the practical competencies required in inclusive classrooms. Participants described feelings of professional unpreparedness, limited access to applicable instructional tools and a need for more sustained experiential learning opportunities. In addition, teachers emphasized the importance of structured professional guidance, mentorship and collaboration with general education teachers, school leadership and parents. Participants also reported that limited resources, insufficient support staff and restricted time for individualized planning constrain their ability to implement inclusive practices effectively. title: Inclusive education for pre‐service physical education teachers: Reflections on Chile's initial teacher training
abstract: Abstract This study analyses how inclusion is addressed in initial teacher training of pre‐service physical education teachers in Chile, exploring the tools provided to address the diversity of students. The perceptions and experiences of programme directors and faculty from four Physical Education teaching programs were examined using a qualitative approach and a case study design, with interviews (26) and focus groups (4) as the primary data collection methods. The results identify three key dimensions for effective inclusive teacher training. The ecological dimension addresses interactions among educational system stakeholders; the human dimension focuses on the attitudes, values and competencies required of pre‐service teachers; and the practical dimension emphasizes concrete experiences in diverse contexts. Furthermore, the importance of initial and continuous training is highlighted, considering the unique characteristics of the subject area and encouraging continuous professional development in inclusion. title: Going beyond academics: Individualised education plan priorities of parents of autistic children in Ireland
abstract: Abstract As the numbers of autistic children attending school in Ireland increases, there is a growing reliance on specialised provision. Individual Education Plans (IEPs) are considered fundamental to this type of educational provision. However, emerging evidence from the Irish context reveals substantial shortcomings in the IEP process. Of particular note is the necessity for significant improvements around aligning educational goals with the actual strengths and needs of autistic children. Therefore, situated within the context of increasing autism class provision and the importance of parental input in the IEP goal‐setting process, our co‐produced research set out to survey the educational priorities of parents of autistic children in Ireland. In total, 48 parents completed the survey. Findings supported a curricular approach whereby functional skills, social inclusion and self‐determination are integrated with academic priorities. Strong parental opposition to goals such as improving eye contact and reducing stimming behaviours was also evident. title: Teaching socio‐communicative behaviours in play routines with caregivers: A feasibility study
abstract: Abstract The first signs of autism often become evident as early as before a child's first birthday, and very early intervention is key to securing optimal outcomes. In the present study, two mother–child dyads participated, with mothers being trained in behavioural strategies targeting socio‐communicative behaviours in their children, who were high‐probability siblings of an older child diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Both mothers demonstrated increased use of naturalistic behavioural strategies and excellent indices of maintenance and generalisation upon the conclusion of training. Children's progress was measured in imitation, respondent joint attention and speaker behaviour, showing promising results in areas of significant concern at intake. Mothers' satisfaction was assessed using a social validity questionnaire, and measures of children's assent were collected, supporting the intervention as feasible and enjoyable for both dyads.

title: Analysing the perspectives of parents of typically developing children on inclusive education in Türkiye within a bioecological framework
abstract: Abstract This study examines the perspectives of parents whose children participate in inclusive classrooms alongside peers with special educational needs (SEN) in Türkiye. Drawing on Bronfenbrenner's Bioecological Systems Theory, this study explores parents' perspectives on inclusive education and the multiple contextual factors shaping inclusive practices. Data were collected through semi‐structured interviews with 21 parents, and thematic analysis identified the following five interconnected themes corresponding to the ecological system levels: (i) conditional and fragile engagement , (ii) inconsistent inclusive practices , (iii) lack of transparent communication , (iv) sympathy constrained by personal boundaries and (v) positive attitudinal shifts over time . The findings indicate that parents generally have a limited understanding of inclusive education, which is conceptualised as a dynamic and context‐dependent process shaped by multiple interacting systems. title: Editorial
Issue Information
Spirituality and academic performance for primary‐aged pupils with special educational needs and disabilities
abstract: Abstract This study investigated the relationship between spirituality and academic performance for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) in primary schools in England. OFSTED provided the statistics on spiritual development of 480,309 pupils in 1668 primary schools in England. These data were analysed with measures of academic performance from the Department for Education's Key Stage 2 – Progress Results (2019). Three regression models determined the extent to which spirituality could predict academic performance. Five educator participants were then interviewed and answered 10 open‐ended questions in relation to spirituality and academic performance. These results identified spirituality as a positive predictor of academic performance. The findings support spiritually cultivated components of learning that function to increase academic performance. It is suggested that spirituality can increase the academic performance of some pupils with SEND, though its impact may depend on factors such as type and severity of need, as well as parental and teacher involvement.

An integrative review (IR) of (intersectional) inclusive pedagogies for students with special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND)
abstract: Abstract The article conducts an integrative review of articles published from 2013 to 2023 that discuss theoretical, empirical and intersectional dimensions of inclusive pedagogies for students with special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND). The aim was to develop an understanding of definitions and applications of SEND‐related inclusive pedagogies to create an integrated mapping of their disparate understandings and applications for this group of students. The following questions guide the analysis: (1) What are the different understandings and enactments of inclusive pedagogies for students designated as having SEND? (2) What is ‘special’ about inclusive pedagogies? (3) In what ways are these pedagogies informed by and address the intersectional needs of students with SEND? The necessity of this analysis lies in the fact that inclusive education reforms necessitate a clear articulation of the meaning and application of inclusive pedagogies in creating effective and non‐discriminatory learning environments for students with SEND who might be located at the intersections of more than one minoritised status. title: Local area strategic leadership to support and enhance the role of SENCos
The line it is drawn; the curse it is cast: A Bourdieusian exploration of inclusion
abstract: Abstract The inclusion of children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) in mainstream schools requires leaders to manage external and internal pedagogical priorities. This paper uses Bourdieu's theoretical toolkit to explore the ways in which inclusion is considered and enacted in UK schools. We look at how school leaders must balance their inclusive priorities with legitimate external pressures of the standards agenda and curriculum learning. We also look at the ways in which a young person may feel unable to meet typical learning and behavioural expectations due to a mismatch in their disposition (habitus) and the success criteria of an educational setting. We suggest that these students may feel pressure to alter their dispositions to better meet the capital requirements of the field, leaving them experiencing hysteresis or feelings of discomfort and a lack of belonging in schools. title: ‘We are different, but we are not really that different’: An insight into the challenges encountered by career leaders when supporting disabled students in English mainstream and specialist classrooms
abstract: Abstract For over 10 years, schools have been responsible for providing career support to all young people. In order for schools to be able to deliver career support in the classroom, the career leader role was introduced as part of the Education Act 2011. With increasing numbers of disabled students attending mainstream school, a key challenge encountered is ensuring that the support provided is inclusive and accessible to all young people. This article provides an overview of a case study which brought together eight educational professionals working across mainstream and specialist provisions. It was hoped that by providing space for these educational practitioners to share practice, they could both reflect on their own experiences and identify ways to develop more inclusive practice when providing career support to young disabled people. As with many of the professionals working within the current English education system, the career leaders demonstrated their commitment to ensuring all young people have opportunities to successfully transition from school; however, they find themselves constrained by a system that is not working. title: ‘I used to walk around the playground wondering where all my friends had gone’: The reflections of how adults with developmental prosopagnosia made friends in childhood
abstract: Abstract Current research into developmental prosopagnosia (DP) estimates a high prevalence rate in the general population, but there exist many gaps in the research. More needs to be learned about the lived experience of those with DP and how to identify it in children. Using reflexive thematic analysis, this study explored the lived experience of how twelve adults with self‐reported DP made and sustained friendships in their childhood. It identified four themes: coping strategies, psychosocial consequences, feelings and advice to others. There were three coping strategies, which had varying success in friendship formation and psychosocial consequences. For many, childhood was an exceedingly challenging time in which they felt uncomfortable with people because they had identification anxiety. The paper concludes that these findings should be used to inform professionals about how they identify DP and to use successful coping strategies to form and sustain friendships.
